title: Base-b Divisibility Rules
description: Generalizes divisibility rules to arbitrary bases: for b ≥ 3, (b-1) | n iff (b-1) | digit_sum_b(n). Covers hexadecimal (mod 15), octal (mod 7), factor tests, and cross-base divisibility. All 15 theorems fully verified.

overview.historicalContext: Divisibility rules have been known since ancient times. The base-10 rule for 3 and 9 was formalized in the parent file. This generalization reveals the universal principle: for ANY base b, the digit sum test works modulo (b-1) and its factors.
overview.problemStatement:
**Base-b Divisibility Rules:**

For b ≥ 3 and n ∈ ℕ:
$$n \equiv \sum_i d_i \pmod{b-1}$$
where $d_i$ are the base-b digits of n.

More generally, for any d ≥ 2 dividing (b-1):
$$d \mid n \iff d \mid \sum_i d_i$$
overview.proofStrategy: The key observation is b ≡ 1 (mod b-1), proved by Euclidean division: b = (b-1)·1 + 1. Then b^k ≡ 1^k = 1 (mod b-1), so n = Σ dᵢ·b^i ≡ Σ dᵢ (mod b-1). For factors d of (b-1), the same logic applies since b ≡ 1 (mod d).
keyInsights: b % (b-1) = 1 is the universal principle behind all digit-sum divisibility tests
In hex: 16 ≡ 1 (mod 15), enabling mod-15, mod-5, and mod-3 tests
Cross-base: 3 | n can be tested via digit sums in base 10, 16, or any base where 3 | (b-1)

conclusion.summary: Complete formalization of base-b divisibility rules with 0 axioms and 0 sorries. The universal principle b ≡ 1 (mod b-1) explains all digit-sum divisibility tests across all bases.
conclusion.implications: Programmers can use digit-sum tests in any base for quick divisibility checks. The cross-base theorem shows that divisibility by 3 can be checked equally well in decimal, hexadecimal, or any base ≡ 1 (mod 3).
openQuestions: Can the alternating digit sum rule (for b+1) be formalized? E.g., 11 | n ↔ alternating digit sum divisible by 11.
